test.name: FAN-pivot plan when direct records are exhausted
test.description: Census records and death certificate have been searched (first plan complete). The skill proposes a new plan that pivots to FAN research — Family, Associates, Neighbors — as a strategy to find indirect parentage evidence: neighbors in the 1850 census who share a surname, witnesses on Patrick's or Thomas's documents, fellow parishioners in church records. Tests the GPS principle of exhaustive search via community network expansion when direct lines stall.

input.user_message: Direct census and vital records haven't proved parentage yet — create a new plan that takes a FAN approach for the parentage question.

judge_context: Background on what the test author was looking for. None of it is a dimension. Grade what it describes inside the dimensions you were given, and do not add one named after anything below.

The author expected at least one FAN-pivot item, meaning a search aimed at associates, neighbors or witnesses rather than at Patrick Flynn directly. Census neighbors sharing the Flynn surname in 1850, witnesses on Thomas Flynn's documents, and fellow parishioners near Flynn entries in church burial or baptism records are all examples of that shape.

The author also expected each FAN item's rationale to explain the FAN connection, so a reader can see how that person or record type widens the evidence network around the parentage question. A FAN item with no stated connection is thinner than one that has it.
The first plan already covered the 1850 census and the death certificate. The author's intent was that new items open new evidence pathways rather than repeat those two record types.

On sequencing: some FAN searches depend on a prior source finishing first — finding a witness name on a death certificate, for instance, before searching for that witness. The author expected that dependency to show up in the rationale or in the ordering.
